content: The strategic information system for the health sector, particularly in the context of HIV, is built upon 12 essential components. These include: 1. Establishing organizational structures with HIV monitoring and evaluation (M&E) functions. 2. Developing human capacity for HIV M&E. 3. Building partnerships to plan, coordinate, and manage the M&E system. 4. Creating a national, multi-sectoral HIV M&E plan. 5. Developing an annual, costed national HIV M&E work plan. 6. Promoting communication, advocacy, and a culture of HIV M&E. 7. Implementing routine HIV program monitoring. 8. Conducting surveys and surveillance activities. 9. Maintaining national and subnational HIV databases. 10. Ensuring supportive supervision and data auditing. 11. Establishing an HIV evaluation and research agenda. 12. Facilitating data dissemination and use. An effective M&E system employs a core set of indicators that are relevant to the program, organizes data collection using standardized forms and aggregation procedures, and streamlines data collection from various sources. Data for monitoring the HIV epidemic and response must come from multiple sources, including facility-generated data (routine patient monitoring and case reporting), surveillance, health facility surveys, administrative sources, population-based surveys, facility assessments, and vital registration systems. These sources collectively provide comprehensive data to monitor the HIV service cascade and global indicators. Facility-generated data, such as patient monitoring and case reporting, form the backbone of data collection. This includes information from laboratory and pharmacy records, which are critical for clinical program management. Administrative data systems, such as financial records, health accounts, and supply chain data, provide insights into the functioning of health systems and service delivery. Population-based surveys, such as demographic and health surveys (DHS) and AIDS indicator surveys (AIS), offer periodic data on general and key populations. Facility assessments, including service availability and readiness assessments (SARA), provide information on the capacity and quality of health services. Vital registration systems record births and deaths, often including causes of death, which are essential for understanding health outcomes. The integration of HIV-related M&E activities into broader health management information systems (HMIS) is a sustainable approach. Key questions for planning and implementing strategic data use include identifying the most relevant indicators for the program, determining the necessary data sources, assessing the capability of data systems to capture and store information, and ensuring data quality and management systems are adequate. It is also crucial to involve all stakeholders, including clinicians, service providers, community programs, and civil society groups, in the M&E system. HIV M&E data should be treated as a public good, accessible to all stakeholders while maintaining high standards of confidentiality and privacy. The use of unique identifiers (UIs) can link data across multiple service delivery points, providing a longitudinal record of individual access to services and clinical outcomes. This also enhances understanding of overall service access, referral efficiency, and epidemiological trends. Challenges in data collection include the complexity and lifelong nature of HIV infection, the need for long-term monitoring, and the difficulty of tracking patients across multiple facilities and service settings. However, well-maintained systems with strong linkages between records can provide critical information for program planning, procurement, and stock management. Outreach data, often maintained by NGOs and community health workers, are vital for linking health facilities with communities. These records provide insights into the reach of HIV prevention services, referrals, and follow-up care. Integrating community data into central reporting systems, while maintaining confidentiality, is essential for comprehensive monitoring. Administrative data systems at the facility level facilitate smooth operations and provide information on service reach, coverage, and quality. These systems include data on human resources, supplies, and service counts. Supervisory visits and quality assessments complement administrative data, identifying gaps in procurement and distribution that may disrupt services. In summary, a robust strategic information system for HIV in the health sector requires the integration of diverse data sources, strong data management systems, and the active involvement of all stakeholders.
